newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU ready to export barley but malt row brewing.
newsitem.headline: EU ready to export barley but malt row brewing.

text.p: The European Commission is ready to supply about half the barley needed to cover a major grain trade deal with Saudi Arabia -- despite accepting only a few bids at its Thursday export tender, officials said.

The EU expects to supply some 200,000 tonnes from its intervention stores, and at Thursday's weekly tender made its remaining stocks available for export. Another 500,000 tonnes could come from the open EU market depending on prices which are "negotiable", they said.
"We are not crazy. Of course we are going to do this business," said one official familiar with EU export policy.
In one of the largest grain deals this year, traders sold 1.4 million tonnes of October-December barley to Saudi Arabia earlier this week for $146-158 a tonne including freight.
Besides the EU, Canada could do 200-400,000 tonnes, the U.S. about half that, Turkey has already sold 125,000 tonnes and Australia could do some if delivery is flexible, sources said.
The EU feels it has the logistical edge and that it can try to be patient, hoping for world prices to recover somewhat and internal ones -- boosted by the Saudi sale -- to lose steam.
This would in turn reduce export subsidy spending and uphold the Commission's policy of curbing domestic grain costs.
But a stronger reason for not moving now, officials said, is an arcane dispute over malt exports, with high stakes for Japanese and other brewers as well as European malt firms.
Malt export refunds are usually linked to the last two barley export refunds each month. The malt export licences have a long validity of the current month plus a further 11 months.

Granting higher refunds for barley on Thursday would have reduced the incentive to bid for the existing malt programme by putting upward pressure on the special malt subsidies, officials said. Japanese importers are already clamouring for such a rise.
The crunch may come when the Commission looks at bids for malt exports in coming days. And according to some officials, it is ready to wave a stick to get its malt programme moving.

"The Commission is waiting for the trade to bid for 1.0 to 1.4 million tonnes of malt on Friday and Monday, profiting from the October increment, and we have to make clear this (malt refund) is an operational level," the EU export source said.
Some officials have begun talking privately of a "negative" brewing premium. This, they implied, would snatch back part of the refund if traders continued to keep the Commission waiting.

The malt refund is an average of recent barley refunds, plus a malting premium (currently zero), then monthly increments of 1.1 Ecus a month where applicable. This sum is multiplied by a coefficient of 1.3 to reach a refund for unroasted malt.
The current refund, set on September 12, is 32.50 Ecus per tonne. Based on the two latest barley refunds averaging 26.07 Ecus, there is already scope for a slight malt refund increase.

Had the Commission covered more sales to Saudi Arabia with export aid straight away (average fob price around $135 per tonne, meaning a refund of over 30 Ecus), it would have had to increase the malt refund, a member-country official said.
This official said he did not know of any plans to claw back higher refunds with a negative malting premium, but such a step would stir up "quite a row" unless clearly justified.
The logic for a negative premium is that the spread between malting and feed barley prices is narrowing after big crops, EU sources said.
Maltsters accuse the EU of overmanaging their industry, while the Commission says it tries to deter speculation.
EU ministers were drawn in earlier this year when Britain pressed for less EU intervention in malt.
The EU exports some 1.7 to 1.8 million tonnes of malt a year but exports are expected to rise to 1.9 million this year.
